messages.subject: Distance sampling burrows
parts:
Dear distance list,

I am helping some colleagues design a survey to monitor the abundance of
active and inactive burrows of a species of endangered rat in
Madagascar. These burrows are easily identifiable but in their forest
habitat, the detectability reduces quite rapidly from a line. As these
burrows do not move (but may change in activity) between years, we were
thinking of using a new configuration of line transects each year, so
that the same burrows were not being sampled repeatedly - and that
pooling across years would be possible for improving the detection
function if encounter rates are very low.

However, it would be beneficial to be able to monitor the fate of
indiviudal burrows over time and only permanet line transects would be
able to do this. Additionally, permanent line transects would sample
less natural variation and produce more precise estimates for monitoring
purposes.

This may be a simple question, but are there any fundamental
problems/consequences of using permanent line transects to estimate the
abundance of stationary objects (that may change in activity between
years) for monitoring purposes?

Your thoughts and advice would be much appreciated.

Regards,

Richard Young

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling burrows
parts:
Richard, there is no problem in principle in having permanent transects
for stationary objects. If the observer records detected burrows
independently of previous visits, then you should be able to pool data
between visits, to increase sample size for estimating the detection
function. However, if you want to monitor individual nests, then you want
the observer to check all burrows previously detected. A few burrows
undetected on previous visits might also be located, so that the detection
function including both burrows previously detected and newly-detected
burrows will be different (wider) than that for previous visits. If
sample size allows, you would need to estimate the detection function
separately for each survey. If it doesn't, you may be able to use the
covariate option in Distance, to put survey number in as a factor
covariate - or possibly as a continuous covariate (perhaps transformed),
assuming that the scale parameter shows an increasing trend with time.

Note that, at say the 2nd survey, 'new' burrows will be one of two types:
some may genuinely be new since the previous visit; others may be burrows
present but missed in the first survey. The latter will tend to be the
less detectable burrows - and predominantly those further from the
transect - so burrows available for detection (having eliminated those
detected in the previous survey) will not be uniformly distributed with
respect to distance from the line, so that a standard distance sampling
analysis that omits previously-detected (and monitored) burrows will be
biased.

Steve
